steps.action:
# The Last Light

Every evening at dusk, Martin climbed the 112 steps.

He had counted them so many times that the number lived in his bones, the way old sailors carry the rhythm of waves long after they've left the sea. One hundred and twelve steps, and at the top, the lamp — wide as a dining table, patient as a saint.

Martin had kept the Harrow Point Light for thirty-one years. He had outlasted two marriages, one storm that took the boathouse completely, and a persistent rumor in town that he had gone strange. People said that about lighthouse keepers. It didn't bother him much anymore.

The work was simple, which he appreciated. Keep the light burning. Log the weather. Watch for ships in distress. In the early years there had been more ships — great tankers and fishing trawlers that passed close enough that he could sometimes see a figure on deck. He would raise his hand. Occasionally someone raised one back.

Now it was mostly automated. The Coast Guard had offered to relieve him of his post three times in the last decade. Three times he had politely declined, and three times they had let him stay, perhaps out of respect, perhaps out of paperwork exhaustion.

On a Tuesday in November, a small sailboat appeared in conditions that made Martin's stomach tighten. The sky had turned the specific shade of green he distrusted. The wind came in hard, sideways gusts. He watched the boat through his binoculars — it was listing, struggling, the sail chaotic.

He fired a flare. He radioed the Coast Guard. Then he stood at the glass and kept the lamp burning, as if his presence at the top of those 112 steps could guide the boat through willpower alone.

It took forty minutes for the rescue crew to reach them. Two people aboard, both recovered, both cold and shaking and alive.

Martin heard about it second-hand from a coast guardsman who stopped in the following morning. He nodded, poured the man coffee, and didn't say much. That evening he climbed the stairs again.

One hundred and twelve steps.

The lamp turned its slow, indifferent circle, throwing light across water that didn't thank anyone for anything. Martin found that reasonable. The sea owed nobody gratitude. You kept the light because ships were out there, because dark was dark, because someone had to stand at the top of the stairs and refuse to leave.

He pulled his coat tighter and watched the horizon go black.

He had no plans to stop.
